items.title: Switching doors doubles your chance of the car
items.claim: Three doors, one car, two goats. Pick a door. Monty (who knows where the car is) opens a different door revealing a goat. Should you switch?
items.prompt: What's the probability of winning if you switch?

options.text: 1/3 — first guess was 1/3, opening a door doesn't change anything
2/3 — your first guess had 1/3 chance of being right, so the remaining unopened door now carries the original 2/3 probability of the OTHER two doors combined
100 percent — Monty's reveal guarantees the win

items.reveal_title: Marilyn vos Savant and a thousand wrong PhDs
items.reveal:
Vos Savant published the answer 'switch' in Parade magazine in 1990. Thousands of readers wrote in — including PhDs in mathematics — insisting she was wrong. She was right.

The key: Monty knows where the car is and always reveals a goat. Your initial choice has 1/3 probability of the car. The OTHER two doors together have 2/3 probability. Monty's reveal removes one of those two doors but doesn't change the 2/3 — it now sits entirely on the remaining unopened door.

If Monty acted randomly (sometimes revealing the car himself), switching wouldn't help — but he doesn't. His knowledge is essential.

The Monty Hall puzzle is the canonical demonstration that conditional probability defeats intuition. Run the simulation 1000 times: switching wins about 667 of them, sticking wins 333.
items.why: Probability intuition assumes 'two outcomes equally likely'. Conditional probability — conditioning on what Monty reveals — distinguishes outcomes that 'look' symmetric but aren't.

items.title: You can estimate pi by dropping a needle on a striped floor
items.claim: A floor has parallel lines spaced apart by distance L. Drop a needle of length L randomly. The probability the needle crosses a line is exactly 2/pi.
items.prompt: Why does pi appear in a problem with no circles?

options.text: The probability calculation involves integrating over the needle's random angle (a continuous variable on [0, pi]) and over its random position (linear), and the integral of sin theta from 0 to pi equals 2 — bringing pi into the denominator
Only works if the floor is circular

items.reveal:
Comte de Buffon set up the problem in 1733. Let d be the perpendicular distance from the needle's centre to the nearest line, and theta the angle the needle makes with the lines. The needle crosses a line if d is less than (L/2) sin theta.

Take d uniform on [0, L/2] and theta uniform on [0, pi/2]. Probability of crossing = (1 / (L/2 * pi/2)) * integral over the crossing region.

Working out: P = (2 / pi). So pi appears because the angle integration covers a full half-period of the sine.

This means you can estimate pi by dropping needles randomly: count crossings out of N drops, multiply by N/(2 * crossings) ≈ pi. Mario Lazzarini reported in 1901 having got pi to six decimals by 3408 throws — almost certainly cherry-picked (six decimals would require billions of throws).

Pi shows up in every probability problem involving a uniform-random angle. The constant of integration smuggles it in.
items.why: Pi is associated with circles. It actually appears in many problems involving angular randomness — anywhere a uniform integration over angles is required.
